title: Parts and wholes, including remaining fractions
transcript: A fraction tells you about a particular whole. When the whole changes, the same fraction can describe a different number of pieces. Draw equal parts for the first whole, then mark which amount becomes the whole for the next instruction.

In AMC practice, a fraction of the original pile and a fraction of what is left can occur in the same problem. Underline the words after of. A Rossmoyne style word puzzle may reveal the ending and ask you to recover the starting quantity. Reverse one change at a time.
There are twenty-four tokens. A player takes one of four equal parts. How many tokens remain? Show the difference between the amount removed and the amount the question asks for.
One part has six tokens. The remaining three parts contain eighteen tokens. Check by adding the removed part back. eighteen plus six returns twenty-four.

A box starts with seventy-two chalk pieces. A class uses one of four equal parts. Then another class uses one of three equal parts of what is left. How many pieces remain after both classes? Label the whole for each fraction.

After the first class the remaining count is fifty-four, since seventy-two divided by four were used. The next whole is now fifty-four. Divide it into three equal parts. The second class uses eighteen pieces. Subtract the second use to get thirty-six. This is two of the second whole's parts.
Take one of four equal parts from a pile. Add a gift of nine pieces. Then take one of three equal parts of that new amount. There are forty-two pieces left. How many were in the original pile?

The ending forty-two pieces represent two of the last three equal parts. Find one part, then rebuild that whole. Undo the gift by subtracting nine. The remaining fifty-four pieces are what was left after the first removal. Those were three of the original four equal parts. Restoring the missing part gives seventy-two.

Run the recipe forward. Remove eighteen from seventy-two to get fifty-four. Add the gift to get sixty-three. The final removal is twenty-one. That leaves forty-two, the stated ending. Each fraction has used its own whole.

Add fractions directly only when they refer to the same original whole. A fraction of what is left uses a new whole. When reversing a removal, divide the remaining amount by the number of remaining parts first. The denominator names the size of the full set of parts.

Write the word original, remaining or new above each fraction. Draw equal parts for that named whole. If the ending is known, rebuild the last whole first. Then reverse any addition and earlier removal.
